subject: chemistry
title: Exothermic and endothermic reactions
welcome_lead: Today's adventure: Exothermic and endothermic reactions — AQA GCSE Chemistry (8462) specification, section 4.5.1.
meta_desc: GCSE Chemistry (AQA) practice covering Exothermic and endothermic reactions, specification section 4.5.1.
final_note: You worked through Exothermic and endothermic reactions — 24 specification statements.

concepts.def: Energy is conserved in chemical reactions: the amount of energy in the universe at the end of a chemical reaction is the same as before the reaction takes place. Energy is only moved between the reacting chemicals and their surroundings.

Everything outside the reacting chemicals themselves, including the solvent, the container and the air. It is the temperature of the surroundings that a thermometer in the reaction mixture actually measures.
A reaction that transfers energy to the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings increases. The product molecules end up with less energy than the reactants, by the amount transferred.
A reaction that takes in energy from the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings decreases.
The reaction of a substance with oxygen, releasing energy. Combustion is exothermic.
A reaction in which a substance gains oxygen. Many oxidation reactions, such as the slow oxidation of iron in a hand warmer, are exothermic.
The reaction of an acid with a base or alkali to form a salt and water. Neutralisation is exothermic.
The breaking down of a compound into simpler substances on heating, for example calcium carbonate into calcium oxide and carbon dioxide. Thermal decompositions are endothermic.
An everyday use of an exothermic reaction: a reaction in a separate compartment of the can transfers energy to the drink and warms it.
An everyday use of an exothermic reaction: iron powder oxidises slowly inside the pack and transfers energy to the surroundings.
A use of an endothermic reaction: the reaction inside the pack takes in energy from the surroundings, so the pack and the injury are cooled.
The rise or fall in temperature measured before and after a reaction. A rise shows an exothermic reaction; a fall shows an endothermic one.
An investigation of the variables that affect temperature changes in reacting solutions, such as acid plus metals, acid plus carbonates, neutralisations and displacement of metals.
Chemical reactions can occur only when reacting particles collide with each other and with sufficient energy; a collision with too little energy does not lead to a reaction.
The minimum amount of energy that particles must have to react. It is the energy needed for a reaction to occur.
An energy level diagram showing the relative energies of reactants and products, the activation energy and the overall energy change, with a curved line showing the energy as the reaction proceeds.
The difference in energy between the reactants and the products, shown on a reaction profile and, at higher tier, calculated from bond energies.
Energy must be supplied to break bonds in the reactants, so bond breaking takes energy in.
Energy is released when bonds in the products are formed.
The energy associated with a particular bond, used to calculate the energy needed to break bonds and the energy released when bonds are formed.

mcqs.q: A reaction transfers energy to the surroundings. What must be true of the product molecules?
options: They have less energy than the reactants, by the amount transferred out.
They have more energy than the reactants, by the amount given out.
They have less energy, and the energy released no longer exists.
They have exactly the same total energy as the reactants did.
mcqs.explain: This is the specification's own statement: the energy that reached the surroundings came from the chemicals, so the products sit lower by exactly that amount.

mcqs.q: Which statement about energy during a chemical reaction is correct?
options: Energy is conserved only in reactions that give energy out to the surroundings.
The total energy in the universe is the same after the reaction as before.
Some of the energy is destroyed as the surroundings are being warmed.
Extra energy is created as the new product molecules are formed.
mcqs.explain: Energy is conserved in chemical reactions; the reaction only moves energy between the chemicals and their surroundings.

mcqs.q: Which statement describes an exothermic reaction?
options: It takes in energy from the surroundings, so their temperature rises.
It transfers energy out, so the temperature of the surroundings falls.
It transfers energy to the surroundings, so their temperature rises.
It stores the energy inside the products, so nothing warms up.
mcqs.explain: This is the specification definition: energy goes out to the surroundings and the temperature of the surroundings increases.

mcqs.q: Which of these reactions is exothermic?
options: the thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate
the reaction inside a sports injury cold pack
citric acid reacting with sodium hydrogencarbonate
the neutralisation of an acid by an alkali
mcqs.explain: Neutralisation is one of the three exothermic examples named by the specification, alongside combustion and many oxidation reactions.

mcqs.q: Magnesium ribbon is lit with a Bunsen flame and burns brightly, warming the tripod above it. Why is this reaction described as exothermic?
options: Energy had to be supplied by the flame, so energy is taken in overall here.
Combustion transfers energy to the surroundings, and that is why the tripod warms.
The oxidation takes in energy from the surrounding air, making it glow.
Burning stores the energy in the magnesium oxide that is produced.
mcqs.explain: Combustion is exothermic; the flame only starts it, and the energy warming the tripod comes out of the chemicals.

mcqs.q: A hand warmer contains iron powder that oxidises slowly once the pack is opened. Why does the pack become warm?
options: The pack takes energy in from your own hand, and this is what makes it warm.
The reaction is endothermic, so it lets out the heat it had stored.
The oxidation is exothermic and transfers energy to your hands and the air.
Slow reactions give out no energy; the padding keeps hands warm.
mcqs.explain: Many oxidation reactions are exothermic, and the specification names hand warmers as an everyday use of one.

mcqs.q: Which statement describes an endothermic reaction?
options: It takes in energy from the surroundings, so their temperature will rise.
It gives out energy, and so the temperature of the surroundings falls.
It releases the energy that was stored inside the reactants.
It takes energy in from the surroundings, so their temperature falls.
mcqs.explain: This is the specification definition: energy is taken in from the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings decreases.

mcqs.q: Copper carbonate is heated strongly and breaks down into copper oxide and carbon dioxide. Why is this reaction endothermic?
options: Energy is taken in to break the compound down.
Energy is given out because a hot flame is used here.
Energy is stored, then released as the gas escapes.
Energy is destroyed as the carbonate breaks apart.
mcqs.explain: Thermal decompositions are endothermic: energy has to be supplied continuously from the surroundings for the compound to break down.

mcqs.q: Citric acid solution is stirred with sodium hydrogencarbonate. The mixture fizzes and the thermometer falls from 21 °C to 15 °C. What does this show?
options: The reaction is exothermic, as the fizzing shows energy leaving.
The reaction is exothermic, since the chemicals have lost energy.
The reaction is endothermic and takes energy in from the surroundings.
No energy was transferred, as 6 °C is too small a change.
mcqs.explain: The temperature of the surroundings has decreased, which is the specification's test for an endothermic reaction; this pair is its named example.

mcqs.q: A student measures the temperature of the surroundings before and after four reactions. Which result shows an endothermic reaction?
options: The temperature rose from 22.0 °C to 31.5 °C during this reaction.
The temperature rose from 16.5 °C to 22.0 °C as it went along.
The temperature stayed at 22.0 °C throughout the reaction.
The temperature fell from 22.0 °C to 16.5 °C during the reaction.
mcqs.explain: A fall in the temperature of the surroundings is exactly how the specification says an endothermic reaction is recognised.

mcqs.q: During a neutralisation the thermometer in the mixture rises by 8 °C. What has happened to the energy?
options: It has been transferred from the chemicals to the surroundings.
It has been transferred from the surroundings and into the chemicals.
It has been created by the acid and alkali as they react together.
It has been stored in the salt and the water that are made.
mcqs.explain: The solution is part of the surroundings, so a rise in its temperature shows energy leaving the chemicals: an exothermic reaction.

mcqs.q: A sports injury pack and a hand warmer each rely on a chemical reaction. Which comparison is correct?
options: The injury pack is exothermic; the hand warmer is endothermic.
The injury pack is endothermic and the warmer exothermic.
Both are exothermic, but the injury pack releases energy slowly.
Both are endothermic, and each takes energy from the skin.
mcqs.explain: The pack must take energy in from the surroundings to cool a swelling, while the warmer must transfer energy out to the hands.

mcqs.q: A self-heating can warms coffee using the reaction of calcium oxide with water. Which property makes this reaction suitable for that use?
options: It is endothermic, so it draws energy out of the air and into the drink.
It is exothermic, so the reacting chemicals themselves become hotter.
It is exothermic, but only when the temperature change is large.
It is exothermic, so it transfers enough energy to warm the drink in the can.
mcqs.explain: An everyday use of an exothermic reaction: energy released by the reaction passes into the drink and raises its temperature.

mcqs.q: In Required practical 4 a student adds different volumes of sodium hydroxide to 25 cm3 of acid and records the highest temperature reached. What is the independent variable?
options: the volume of sodium hydroxide added
the highest temperature that is reached
the concentration of the acid used
the insulation of the plastic cup
mcqs.explain: It is the variable the student deliberately chooses and changes; the highest temperature is what is measured as a result.

mcqs.q: Why is the reacting mixture in Required practical 4 placed in a polystyrene cup with a lid?
options: to hold the mixture at a steady temperature all through the reaction
to reduce the energy transferred to and from the surroundings
to make the reaction go faster so that a change can be seen sooner
to stop the temperature of the room from changing at all
mcqs.explain: Polystyrene insulates and the lid limits evaporation, so more of the energy change shows up as a temperature change in the mixture.

mcqs.q: Two reactant particles collide with each other but no reaction takes place. What is the reason?
options: Every collision must react, so this cannot happen.
They collided with less than the energy given out here.
They collided with too little energy to react.
The reaction is exothermic, so no energy is needed.
mcqs.explain: Reactions occur only when particles collide with sufficient energy; a collision below the activation energy simply bounces apart.

mcqs.q: What is meant by the activation energy of a reaction?
options: the minimum amount of energy that particles must have in order to react
the energy that the product molecules are left with at the very end
the total amount of energy the reaction gives out overall
the energy released whenever two reactant particles collide
mcqs.explain: This is the specification's definition of the activation energy, word for word in substance.

mcqs.q: Which set of quantities can be shown on a reaction profile?
options: the relative energies of the reactants and the products and the time that the whole reaction takes to finish
the relative energies of the reactants and products, the activation energy and the overall energy change
the activation energy on its own, because the products are not marked anywhere on the diagram
the temperature of the surroundings measured before and after the reaction has finished
mcqs.explain: These are precisely the three things the specification says a reaction profile can be used to show.

mcqs.q: A student draws a reaction profile for an endothermic reaction. Which description of the drawing is correct?
options: The products line lies below the reactants, joined by a curve with a peak.
A straight sloping line runs from the reactants line up to the products.
The products line lies above the reactants, joined by a curved peak.
The top of the curve is level with the products line on the right.
mcqs.explain: Endothermic products are higher in energy than the reactants, and the specification asks for a curved line passing over the activation energy peak.

mcqs.q: A reaction profile shows the products at a lower energy than the reactants. What does this tell you about the reaction?
options: It is endothermic and takes in energy overall.
It is exothermic only if the peak is low.
It cannot happen, as products must be higher.
It is exothermic and gives out energy.
mcqs.explain: Products lower than reactants means the chemicals have lost energy, and that energy has gone to the surroundings.

mcqs.q: Why must colliding particles have at least the activation energy?
options: because it is the energy the reaction gives to the surroundings
because it is the energy that is needed for the reaction to occur
because it is only needed when a reaction is endothermic
because it is the energy needed to make particles collide
mcqs.explain: The specification puts it in exactly these terms: the activation energy is the energy needed for a reaction to occur.

mcqs.q: During a chemical reaction, what happens to the bonds in the reactants?
options: Energy is released as each one of them breaks.
They break with no energy change at all.
Energy must be supplied so that they break.
They break once new bonds have formed.
mcqs.explain: The specification states that energy must be supplied to break bonds in the reactants, so bond breaking takes energy in.

mcqs.q: What happens to energy when the bonds in the products are formed?
options: Energy is released only if it is exothermic.
Energy must be supplied to make them form.
Energy is stored and none gets out.
Energy is released as these bonds form.
mcqs.explain: The specification states that energy is released when bonds in the products are formed.

mcqs.q: A student is given a table of bond energies for a reaction. What can these values be used to calculate?
options: the energy taken in breaking bonds and released forming them
the total energy of the reaction, by adding up every value in the table
the number of bonds broken and the number of bonds formed in total
the temperature rise when the reaction is done in a glass beaker
mcqs.explain: Bond energies give both sums the specification names: the energy needed to break bonds and the energy released when bonds are formed.

mcqs.q: How is the overall energy change of a reaction found from bond energies?
options: the sum of the energy released forming bonds minus the sum needed to break
the sum of the energy needed to break bonds added to the sum released
the sum of the energy needed to break bonds minus the sum released forming bonds
the number of bonds broken subtracted from the number of bonds made
mcqs.explain: This is the specification's definition of the overall energy change: the difference between the two sums, taken in that order.

mcqs.q: H2 + Cl2 → 2HCl. Bond energies in kJ/mol: H–H 436, Cl–Cl 242, H–Cl 431. What is the overall energy change?
options: +1540 kJ/mol, adding all the values up
+184 kJ/mol, so it is endothermic
+247 kJ/mol, using one H-Cl bond
-184 kJ/mol, so this is exothermic
mcqs.explain: Breaking: 436 + 242 = 678. Forming: 2 x 431 = 862. Overall energy change = 678 - 862 = -184 kJ/mol, so energy is given out.

mcqs.q: In an exothermic reaction, how do the two bond energy sums compare?
options: Forming new bonds releases more than breaking bonds needs.
Breaking existing bonds needs more than forming new bonds gives out.
More bonds are formed in the products than are broken overall.
The two sums are equal, so no energy is left over here.
mcqs.explain: The specification states that in an exothermic reaction the energy released from forming new bonds is greater than the energy needed to break existing bonds.

mcqs.q: A reaction is endothermic. What does this tell you about the bond energy sums?
options: More bonds are broken than are formed in this reaction.
Breaking bonds needs more than forming lets out.
Forming bonds gives out more than breaking needs.
No bonds are formed, so no energy can be given out.
mcqs.explain: The specification states that in an endothermic reaction the energy needed to break existing bonds is greater than the energy released from forming new bonds.

specSource: AQA GCSE Chemistry (8462) specification; section 4.5.1 Exothermic and endothermic reactions
